articles.title: Sonezão, fundador da Junco e referência do empreendedorismo em Uberlândia, morre aos 94 anos | G1
articles.standfirst: Fundador da empresa criada em Uberlândia em 1991, Onésimo Domingos Costa transformou um negócio familiar em uma marca com distribuição em todo o país. A Prefeitura decretou três dias de luto oficial.
articles.summary: Fundador da empresa criada em Uberlândia em 1991, Onésimo Domingos Costa transformou um negócio familiar em uma marca com distribuição em todo o país.
articles.body:
Onésimo Domingos Costa, o Sonezão, fundador da Junco — Foto: Redes sociais/reprodução

Morreu nesta quarta-feira (30), aos 94 anos, Onésimo Domingos Costa, conhecido como Sonezão , fundador da Junco, empresa do setor de alimentos criada em Uberlândia em 1991. A Prefeitura de Uberlândia decretou três dias de luto oficial pela morte do empresário .

O velório ocorre desde as 8h desta quinta-feira (1º), na Sala Espaço Nobre da Paz Universal, no Bairro Brasil. O sepultamento será às 17h, no Cemitério São Pedro .

O empresário deixa a esposa, Divina da Costa; os filhos Ana Helena Junqueira, Roque Domingos Junqueira, Paulo Romes Junqueira, Onésimo Domingos Filho e Júnio Domingos Junqueira; além de netos e bisnetos.

Pelas redes sociais, o filho Paulo Romes Junqueira, secretário de Trânsito e Transportes de Uberlândia e presidente da Junco, compartilhou mensagens lamentando a morte do pai e uma imagem que mostra o crachá de Sonezão como presidente-fundador da empresa.

A Junco, referência nacional nos segmentos de artigos para festas, guloseimas, condimentos e produtos naturais, também publicou uma homenagem ao fundador nas redes sociais.

“Nosso querido Sonezão foi muito mais que o fundador da Junco. Com coragem, trabalho e um grande sonho, construiu os primeiros capítulos de uma história que hoje faz parte da vida de tantas pessoas. Fica nossa eterna admiração e gratidão por tudo o que construiu, ensinou e deixou como legado. Seguiremos honrando seus valores e mantendo vivo o sonho que começou com ele”.

Sonezão começou vendendo de porta em porta

A história da Junco começou há mais de 30 anos, quando Onésimo Domingos decidiu vender temperos e condimentos de porta em porta. O crescimento da empresa familiar é considerado inspirador.

Atualmente, a empresa mantém uma indústria em Uberlândia e produz artigos para festas, alimentos naturais, condimentos, balas de coco, doces, velas e itens de confeitaria distribuídos por todo o país.

articles.title: Emirados Árabes abrem investigação sobre ataque em voo da FlyDubai | G1
articles.standfirst: Voo da FlyDubai fazia rota entre Dubai e Tel Aviv, mas desviou e pousou na Arábia Saudita. Passageiros e tripulação ajudaram a conter copiloto, que esfaqueou piloto. Israel disse que caso foi uma tentativa de atentado terrorista.
articles.summary: Voo da FlyDubai fazia rota entre Dubai e Tel Aviv, mas desviou e pousou na Arábia Saudita. Passageiros e tripulação ajudaram a conter copiloto, que esfaqueou piloto. Israel disse que caso foi uma tentativa de atentado terrorista.
articles.body:
O procurador-geral dos Emirados Árabes Unidos anunciou nesta quinta-feira (1) a abertura de uma investigação sobre o incidente ocorrido a bordo de um voo da FlyDubai que seguia para Israel, informou a imprensa estatal.

A agência WAM destacou que "a equipe de investigação começou a trabalhar no incidente" e que seu trabalho determinará se este "poderia estar vinculado a alguma atividade ou tentativa terrorista".

Segundo políticos israelenses e vários passageiros, um dos pilotos do avião esfaqueou na quarta-feira o outro copiloto e tentou derrubar a aeronave. O piloto e alguns passageiros impediram que o avião caísse após o ataque.

Passageiros ensanguentados após briga entre pilotos em voo da Flydubai rumo a Israel que foi desviado para a Arábia Saudita em 30 de setembro de 2026. — Foto: Reprodução/redes sociais

A investigação permitirá determinar até que ponto o incidente "estava vinculado a alguma atividade ou intenção terrorista", segundo a WAM.

A companhia aérea FlyDubai informou que os 174 passageiros, incluindo 166 israelenses, estavam a salvo.

Autoridades israelenses classificaram o incidente como "uma tentativa de ataque terrorista". O primeiro-ministro Benjamin Netanyahu disse ao canal americano Fox News que é "muito cedo" para dizer quem é responsável pelos fatos.

"Durante o voo, ao se aproximar do país, um dos pilotos esfaqueou o outro e aparentemente tentou derrubar o avião com todos a bordo", comentou Netanyahu.

Israel também realiza uma investigação própria sobre o ataque, com a agência de inteligência Mossad à frente dos esforços de apuração.

Uma mulher carrega um cachorro enquanto passageiros que estavam no voo da Flydubai com destino a Israel, saído dos Emirados Árabes Unidos e desviado para a Arábia Saudita após emitir um sinal de emergência. — Foto: Ammar Awad / Reuters

Infográfico mostra rota de avião que tinha Tel Aviv como destino mas desviou após copiloto atacar piloto, no que o governo de Israel classificou como tentativa de ataque terrorista, em 30 de setembro de 2026. — Foto: arte/ g1

articles.title: Governo Trump destina US$ 1 milhão para contestar STF no Brasil | G1
articles.standfirst: Verba faz parte de pacote de US$ 176,9 milhões do Departamento de Estado para projetos que incluem iniciativas de direita e conservadoras em vários países
articles.summary: O governo Trump destinou US$ 1 milhão para contestar o STF e a censura no Brasil, integrando um fundo do Departamento de Estado para projetos conservadores globais.
articles.body:
Foto de arquivo: Trump com o secretário de Estado, Marco Rubio, no Salão Oval da Casa Branca, em Washington, D.C, em 16 de julho de 2025. — Foto: Reuters/Nathan Howard

Os Estados Unidos destinaram US$ 1 milhão a um projeto que financia grupos da sociedade civil contrários ao que o governo americano descreve como excesso de poder judicial e censura por parte do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) , segundo uma reportagem publicada pelo jornal britânico "The Guardian".

A verba faz parte de um pacote de US$ 176,9 milhões (cerca de R$ 917 milhões) em 43 concessões do Fundo de Direitos Humanos e Democracia (HRDF, na sigla em inglês) do Departamento de Estado dos EUA. Segundo o "Guardian", os recursos foram destinados a projetos que incluem iniciativas de direita e conservadoras em diferentes países.

O projeto relacionado ao Brasil é chamado de “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” (“Combatendo a guerra jurídica e a censura no Brasil”, em tradução livre). De acordo com um documento visto pelo jornal, a iniciativa financiaria organizações da sociedade civil que se opõem ao que o programa classifica como excesso de poder judicial e censura por parte do STF.

O jornal britânico afirma que a iniciativa faz parte de uma mudança na forma como o governo de Donald Trump direciona recursos do fundo. A nova lista inclui projetos relacionados a temas como imigração, anticomunismo, proteção de cristãos, oposição à chamada “ideologia de gênero” e críticas à regulamentação.

O pacote também inclui uma concessão de US$ 40 milhões para um consórcio liderado pela "Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation", organização sem fins lucrativos anticomunista .

Segundo o jornal, integrantes do governo Trump defenderam pessoalmente algumas das concessões. Um assessor democrata do Congresso americano afirmou que a senadora Jeanne Shaheen havia mantido bloqueios sobre US$ 22 milhões em concessões, incluindo recursos destinados ao Brasil, à África do Sul, à Nigéria e à promoção de uma ideologia de direita no Reino Unido e na Europa.

Ainda segundo o assessor, o secretário de Estado americano, Marco Rubio , assinou pessoalmente um memorando para desconsiderar os bloqueios e liberar os recursos.

O Departamento de Estado não comentou concessões específicas . Em resposta ao "Guardian", afirmou que os programas ainda estavam em “deliberação ativa” e que os beneficiários precisariam atender às regras para concessões federais. O departamento também disse que todos os programas passariam por um processo de verificação.

Quem ainda não participou de nenhuma corrida de rua em Salvador neste ano, ainda tem tempo: pelo menos seis provas estão confirmadas até dezembro, em diversos bairros da cidade. Há opções de 5 km, 10 km e até 15 km.

Aumento de casos de sarampo em São Paulo acende alerta para outros estados; entenda o risco de disseminação — Foto: Adobe Stock

O estado de São Paulo chegou a 40 casos confirmados de sarampo em 2026, segundo balanço do Centro de Vigilância Epidemiológica (CVE) estadual. Três novos casos foram confirmados nesta terça-feira (28), todos em moradores da capital paulista.

Os novos pacientes são dois homens, de 18 e 21 anos, e uma bebê de 1 ano. Segundo o CVE, eles estão ligados a cadeias de transmissão já identificadas e acompanhadas pelas autoridades sanitárias desde junho.

Dos 40 casos registrados no estado, 36 são na cidade de São Paulo, dois em São Bernardo do Campo, um em Guarulhos e um em Santo André. Nenhum paciente morreu.

Cerca de 60% dos casos ocorreram em crianças menores de 2 anos, faixa etária considerada mais vulnerável ao vírus.

Segundo o governo estadual, 30 dos 40 pacientes não tinham registro de vacinação contra o sarampo ou estavam com o esquema vacinal incompleto.

Entre os três novos casos, o homem de 21 anos e a bebê de 1 ano têm uma dose registrada da vacina. O paciente de 18 anos não tem registro de vacinação. O número de doses necessárias varia conforme a idade.

O monitoramento das cadeias de transmissão identificadas desde junho aponta uma tendência de redução da circulação do vírus, segundo o CVE.

Em Guarulhos e São Bernardo do Campo, as autoridades acompanham a possibilidade de considerar encerradas as cadeias de transmissão associadas aos casos registrados nos municípios.

Para que uma cadeia seja considerada interrompida, é necessário passar 90 dias — ou 12 semanas — sem novos casos relacionados, contados a partir do início das manchas na pele do último paciente confirmado.

Durante esse período, as equipes continuam investigando casos suspeitos, rastreando contatos e realizando busca ativa.

Segundo o estado, mais de 1,7 mil notificações suspeitas de sarampo já foram descartadas em 2026.

As investigações incluem exames realizados pelo Instituto Adolfo Lutz e, nos casos confirmados, sequenciamento do genótipo do vírus com apoio da Fiocruz.

A diretora do CVE-SP, Tatiana Lang D'Agostini, afirmou que, nos municípios com casos confirmados, as equipes continuam acompanhando pessoas que tiveram contato com os pacientes e realizando bloqueios vacinais quando indicados pela investigação epidemiológica.

Brasil mantém status de eliminação do sarampo

Apesar dos registros em São Paulo, Amazonas e Rio de Janeiro neste ano, o Brasil mantém o status de eliminação da transmissão endêmica do sarampo.

Segundo o governo paulista, a Organização Pan-Americana da Saúde (Opas) classifica a situação do país e de São Paulo como de transmissão limitada, com casos esporádicos, cadeias identificadas e medidas de contenção em andamento.

Uma primeira cadeia registrada entre março e abril, relacionada a dois casos importados, já foi considerada encerrada após completar 12 semanas sem novos casos associados. Outras cadeias identificadas em junho, julho e agosto continuam sendo monitoradas.

O sarampo é uma doença respiratória altamente contagiosa. Uma pessoa infectada pode transmitir o vírus antes mesmo do aparecimento das manchas vermelhas na pele, um dos principais sinais da doença.

Dados do governo estadual apontam crescimento da cobertura vacinal contra o sarampo em 2026. A cobertura da primeira dose passou de 86,56% em abril para 93,24% em julho. A da segunda dose subiu de 72,72% para 78,37% no mesmo período.

Segundo o estado, mais de 2,5 milhões de doses contra o sarampo foram aplicadas durante a Campanha de Multivacinação em setembro. Esses dados ainda não foram incorporados ao cálculo mais recente da cobertura vacinal.

A vacina está disponível gratuitamente nas unidades básicas de saúde dos 645 municípios paulistas.

O esquema prevê duas doses para crianças, aos 12 e 15 meses. Pessoas de 15 meses a 29 anos devem ter duas doses comprovadas; entre 30 e 59 anos, é necessária pelo menos uma. Trabalhadores da saúde devem comprovar duas doses, independentemente da idade.

Em São Paulo, Guarulhos, São Bernardo do Campo e Santo André, crianças entre 6 e 11 meses e 29 dias também recebem a chamada “dose zero”. A aplicação adicional busca proteger bebês durante o período de circulação do vírus e não substitui as doses de rotina aos 12 e 15 meses.

articles.title: Disapproving nuns painted over the risqué frescoes in Rome's long-neglected Villa Silvestri Rivaldi for 300 years; restorers are now exposing them
articles.summary: For nearly three centuries, layers of plain paint and plaster hid a remarkable secret inside one of Rome’s long-neglected Renaissance villas.
articles.body: For nearly three centuries, layers of plain paint and plaster hid a remarkable secret inside one of Rome’s long-neglected Renaissance villas. Now, restorers peeling back those layers are bringing colourful scenes of gods, goddesses, soldiers and mythological figures back into view, as per a report by Smithsonian Magazine.The rediscovered artwork is inside Villa Silvestri Rivaldi, a sprawling 16th-century residence just a short distance from Rome’s Colosseum. The villa was acquired by Italy’s Lazio region for €25 million in 2024, and an extensive restoration is now revealing frescoes that had been deliberately covered after the property passed into the hands of a religious institution.The murals include nude and semi-nude figures from non-Christian mythology, which reportedly offended the nuns who occupied the villa from the 17th century. The paintings were subsequently plastered over, leaving the Renaissance artwork hidden for around 300 years. Today, conservators are carefully removing those later layers using techniques including laser cleaning and water-based methods. In some sections, the process has already revealed entire scenes that had disappeared from view for generations.Frescoes hidden behind plain wallsVilla Silvestri Rivaldi was built between 1534 and 1547, when Rome was undergoing a major artistic and architectural transformation. Its builder was Eurialo Silvestri, a chamberlain and close associate of Pope Paul III, who hoped the grand residence would help strengthen his ambitions of becoming a cardinal.Although that ambition did not succeed, the villa became home to a succession of prominent figures and families, including members of the Medici and Colonna dynasties. Alessandro de’ Medici, who later became Pope Leo XI, was among those associated with the property.The villa was designed to reflect the wealth and status of its occupants. Its interiors featured elaborate decorations, coats of arms and mythological imagery, while its gardens once included a large nymphaeum with 12 fountains, shell mosaics, statues and orange trees.Its location, overlooking parts of ancient Rome, also influenced the themes chosen by the artists. Classical mythology and ancient Roman imagery were particularly suited to a residence built amid the ruins and monuments of the city.But the villa's artistic character changed dramatically after 1660, when it became the property of the Conservatory of the Mendicant Spinsters. The religious institution operated a girls’ school and orphanage there and remained associated with the building for about three centuries.During that period, the nuns objected to the nude figures and other pagan imagery decorating the walls. Instead of allowing the controversial images to remain visible, the murals were covered. For centuries, the Renaissance paintings effectively disappeared behind the new surfaces.A hidden Renaissance gallery re-emergesThe first serious attempts to uncover the paintings began more than two decades ago. Between 2002 and 2006, conservators carried out cleaning tests on parts of the walls after suspecting that older murals were hidden underneath.Those tests confirmed that significant artwork remained beneath the overpainting. But restoration could not proceed at the time because the villa was still owned by a religious order that did not have the funds required for the work, according to Paola Mezzadri, a conservator and restorer involved in the project.The situation changed after Lazio acquired the property in 2024.Restoration work has now moved into a more substantial phase, with teams stabilising the deteriorating building while simultaneously investigating and cleaning its historic decoration. The wider restoration project has been described as a roughly $40-million effort, including the property acquisition and work intended to give the complex a new public life.One of the most striking discoveries is in the Hall of Divinities. There, restorers have uncovered monumental figures of goddesses, depicted in vibrant oranges, yellows and greens. Some appear with flowing robes while others hold armour or weapons. The scenes offer a glimpse of the elaborate mythological decoration that once transformed the villa’s interiors.Researchers believe Prospero Fontana may have been responsible for at least some of the paintings. Art historians have also linked the decoration to Perino del Vaga, an important artist of the period and a pupil of Raphael’s circle. Drawings preserved at the British Library have helped researchers investigate the possible connection between Fontana and the frescoes.More paintings still waiting to be uncoveredThe Hall of Divinities is not the only part of the villa yielding surprises. In the Hall of the Emperors, restorers are uncovering scenes showing soldiers, cavalry, battles and even a lion. Portraits of Roman emperors, including Titus and Hadrian, have also emerged as layers covering the walls are removed. Another section, known as the Hall of Cupid and Psyche, has yet to be fully investigated.The work is painstaking because restorers have to distinguish between layers of later paint and the original artwork without damaging the fragile frescoes underneath. Modern techniques, including lasers and water-based cleaning methods, are being used to remove the overpaint while limiting the use of chemicals.The villa’s story also extends far beyond the Renaissance. After the nuns left around 1970, the complex went through several later uses and periods of neglect. It became a centre for community arts and political activism and was eventually occupied by squatters.Restorers have even found 20th-century graffiti alongside the centuries-old frescoes, creating an unusual record of the building’s successive lives.For now, there is no fixed date for the villa’s complete restoration or for its eventual public opening. Researchers say the scale of the work means discoveries are still being made as restoration progresses.What was once hidden behind plain walls is slowly becoming visible again: a Renaissance gallery of mythological scenes that survived centuries of changing tastes, religious objections, neglect and abandonment.And after roughly 300 years behind layers of paint and plaster, the figures that the nuns once wanted hidden are finally returning to the walls of Villa Silvestri Rivaldi.You use AI every day. articles.title: Gandhi Jayanti speech ideas: 6 thought-provoking topics students can speak about beyond truth and non-violence
articles.summary: Gandhi Jayanti is marked in schools with speeches about truth, non-violence and cleanliness.
articles.body: Gandhi Jayanti is marked in schools with speeches about truth, non-violence and cleanliness. Gandhi Jayanti is observed every year on October 2 to mark the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi, the leader of India’s freedom movement and the father of the nation. Mahatma Gandhi’s life also raises questions about courage, disagreement, self-discipline, simplicity and the responsibility to act when something feels wrong. For students, these ideas can make a Gandhi Jayanti speech more thoughtful and relevant to everyday life.Gandhi’s idea of non-violence in a world of angry wordsNon-violence is often reduced to “not hurting anyone physically.” Gandhi’s idea was broader. His approach, known as ahimsa, also involved controlling anger and refusing to answer hatred with hatred.A student can connect this with school life. Arguments between friends, hurtful comments and online bullying may not involve physical violence, but words can leave lasting wounds. A speech can explore whether staying calm during disagreement is actually a form of courage.A useful line from Gandhi is: “An eye for an eye only ends up making the whole world blind.”What does truth mean when telling the truth is difficult?Gandhi famously made truth central to his life and political philosophy. He described his experiments with truth in his autobiography, The Story of My Experiments with Truth.This gives students a more interesting speech topic than simply saying, “Always speak the truth.” The speech can ask what happens when honesty has a cost. Admitting a mistake, returning something that does not belong to someone or refusing to copy homework can require more courage than it appears.The focus can be on truth as a daily habit, rather than just a moral lesson repeated on Gandhi Jayanti.Gandhi and the power of ordinary actionsOne of the most relatable Gandhi Jayanti themes is the idea that change does not always begin with a grand gesture.Gandhi encouraged people to take responsibility for their own actions and surroundings. Students can connect this idea with simple choices: wasting food, throwing rubbish, using water carelessly or ignoring someone who needs help.This topic can also move beyond the familiar cleanliness message. The real question is whether people practise values when nobody is watching.Can simplicity make life richer?Gandhi deliberately chose a simple lifestyle and became closely associated with khadi and the charkha. His clothing and way of living were also connected to his wider ideas about self-reliance and economic independence.Students can use this as an opportunity to discuss modern life. Does having more things always mean having a better life? Could buying less, wasting less and valuing what is already available make everyday life more meaningful?The speech need not reject technology or modern comforts. Instead, it can explore the difference between having something and actually needing it.Gandhi’s idea of being the changeThe popular saying, “Be the change that you wish to see in the world,” is widely associated with Gandhi, although that exact wording does not appear as a simple sentence in his writings.A speech can therefore use the underlying idea carefully rather than presenting the quotation as an exact Gandhi statement.For students, the message is powerful. Complaining about litter while dropping a wrapper, demanding kindness while insulting others or asking for honesty while cheating creates a gap between values and behaviour.Gandhi’s life provides a useful starting point for discussing why personal example matters.Gandhi Jayanti: remembering a person, not just a portraitPerhaps the most thoughtful speech could focus on how Gandhi is remembered.Every year, students may see his photograph, hear familiar slogans and participate in school programmes. But remembering a historical figure should involve more than repeating a few famous lines.Gandhi remains a complex historical figure, and his ideas and actions have been debated and criticised from different perspectives. A mature student speech can acknowledge that history without turning the occasion into either blind praise or dismissal.The stronger lesson is to study his choices, understand the context in which he made them and ask what those ideas mean today.Why these speech topics can work for studentsA Gandhi Jayanti speech becomes memorable when it sounds connected to real life. Instead of filling two minutes with dates and slogans, students can take one idea from Gandhi’s life and bring it into the world around them.That could mean discussing how to disagree without cruelty, admit mistakes, resist peer pressure or live with greater responsibility. These are not only history lessons. They are questions students encounter every day.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. articles.title: Was Iran behind the flydubai flight incident? Netanyahu answers
articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said it is “too early” to determine whether Iran was involved in the failed apparent bid to hijack a
articles.body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said it is “too early” to determine whether Iran was involved in the failed apparent bid to hijack a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv.Also Read | 'Used last of his energy': How Captain Machchhar’s quick thinking helped save over 170 lives“Well, it’s too early to say,” Netanyahu told Fox News on Wednesday when asked whether there was any indication of Iranian involvement.“The attacking pilot is now being investigated in Saudi Arabia. I believe the suspect would be taken to the UAE and that Israel could also participate in the investigation,” he added.Netanyahu, however, claimed that “it’s no secret” that Iran wants to target Israelis both abroad and in Israel.“It’s no secret that Iran wants to target Israelis abroad, wants to target Israel here,” the Israeli premier said.Also Read | Captain Machchhar, a dentist, plumber & the crew who helped save over 170 lives on flydubai flightNetanyahu also pointed to "signs" from Tehran’s proxies of plans to carry out attacks in Israel, specifically citing Hamas and Hezbollah ahead of the country’s October 27 elections.“We have clear evidence of that (the alleged plan). But I think that whether or not this was carried out as part of that plan, that we don’t know yet,” he added.Wednesday’s incident came ahead of the third anniversary of Hamas’ October 7, 2023, attacks on Israel. It also occurred amid the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran, which began on February 28.Israel and Iran had also fought a 12-day war in June 2025, during which the US intervened militarily in support of its ally Israel.Smit Machchhar, an Indian national piloting flydubai flight FZ 1073 to Tel Aviv, was seriously wounded after his co-pilot, reportedly an Omani national, stabbed him mid-air. Before collapsing, Machchhar managed to alert Israeli authorities and open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and overpower the attacker.According to the BBC, two off-duty flydubai pilots who were travelling on the same flight took control of the aircraft and made an emergency landing at Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport, where the plane was diverted.Around 180 passengers, most of them Israelis, were on board the flight. They were later flown to Tel Aviv on a second aircraft arranged by the UAE-based airline.Machchhar is undergoing treatment at a hospital in Saudi Arabia. According to the Indian Embassy, his condition is stable.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Japan raises permanent residency fee 20-fold as foreign population hits record
articles.summary: Japan has raised the fee for foreigners seeking permanent residency 20-fold, from 10,000 yen to 200,000 yen, as the government tightens the requirements
articles.body: Japan has raised the fee for foreigners seeking permanent residency 20-fold, from 10,000 yen to 200,000 yen, as the government tightens the requirements for those seeking to settle in the country permanently.The new fee took effect on October 1. Applications submitted by September 30 remain subject to the old 10,000-yen charge, even if approval comes after the fee change.The steep increase is part of a broader overhaul of Japan's permanent residency system. Revised guidelines introduce stricter standards on income and pension eligibility, while a Japanese-language requirement is also being introduced. Most of the new criteria will apply to applications filed from April 2027, although the revised income standard can apply to applications submitted as early as April 2026.Why is Japan tightening permanent residency rules?The changes come as Japan's foreign resident population reaches record levels. There were 4.125 million foreign residents in Japan at the end of 2025, according to the Immigration Services Agency, up from about 2.23 million a decade earlier.The government has linked the fee increases to the rising administrative burden of managing a growing foreign population. A bill enacted in May raised the statutory ceiling for permanent residency fees from 10,000 yen to 300,000 yen, allowing the government to set the actual charge at 200,000 yen.Prime minister Sanae Takaichi's government has made the management of immigration and the integration of foreign residents a policy priority, while Japan continues to rely on overseas workers amid an ageing population and labour shortages.Applicants must now demonstrate that they can support themselves financially, with the revised guidelines requiring income to continuously exceed the average for Japanese households of a comparable size.Pension requirements have also been tightened. Applicants' projected pension benefits must meet a benchmark equivalent to what a person would receive after 30 years in the employees' pension system at the relevant income level. Those whose projected benefits fall short can have savings and other assets taken into account.Japanese-language ability is another new element. The revised guidelines include Japanese proficiency among the factors considered in permanent residency screening, with most of the new requirements taking effect for applications from April 2027.The changes build on earlier tightening of the system. In February, Japan revised its permanent residency guidelines to make screening stricter for applicants with a history of unpaid taxes and social insurance or healthcare premiums, even if those payments were subsequently made.The fee increase triggered a rush at immigration offices in the days before it took effect.Tokyo's main immigration bureau was packed with foreign residents on September 28, with applicants reporting waits of up to 7½ hours as they tried to complete procedures before the new fees came into force.Those unable to submit applications before the deadline now face the new 200,000-yen fee.Some applicants who meet specific criteria can receive a reduction. Under the new system, eligible permanent residency applicants can pay 20,000 yen instead, while certain categories can qualify for fee exemptions.Japan is getting stricter as it gets more dependentThe country is dealing with an ageing population and labour shortages that have increased its reliance on foreign workers, even as the rapid growth in the number of foreign residents has fuelled debate over immigration and integration.Takaichi has said her government wants an "orderly inclusive society" and has backed measures aimed at helping foreign residents understand Japanese language, culture and social rules. A government working group has been examining a structured Japanese-language and social-orientation programme for foreign residents, with a trial planned for fiscal 2028.The result is a two-track approach: Japan continues to bring in foreign workers to help address demographic and labour pressures, while raising the financial, administrative and integration standards for those seeking to remain permanently.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2023, British engineers began using supercritical water to break mixed plastic into hydrocarbons; the plant was designed for 20,000 tonnes a year and was estimated to save 1.8 tonnes of CO₂ per tonne treated
articles.summary: In a groundbreaking initiative, British engineers at Mura Technology leverage supercritical water to recycle difficult plastics, aiming to reduce carbon emissions and tackle plastic waste effectively.
articles.body: Plastic recycling works best when waste is clean, sorted and made from a single polymer. Mixed packaging, films and contaminated plastics are much harder to process and often end up being incinerated or sent to landfill. In 2023, a British company began experimenting with a different approach at Teesside, using water at extremely high temperatures and pressures to break down difficult plastic waste into hydrocarbons that could be used again in manufacturing.According to Reuters, the facility developed by Mura Technology at Wilton International was designed to process 20,000 tonnes of plastic waste a year in its first phase. Rather than burning the material, its HydroPRS process uses supercritical water to break the plastic down into hydrocarbons. These outputs can then be separated and used as chemical feedstock for new plastic and other products.Using water under extreme conditionsThe process starts with plastic waste that is difficult to recycle mechanically using conventional methods. These include films, flexible packaging, pots, tubs, and trays, even those which consist of mixed types of plastics. After preparation, the waste is subjected to water superheated above its critical point of 373 degrees Celsius and pressurised to more than 220 bars. In this state, water behaves differently from liquid water. It becomes a solvent that breaks long-chain polymers into short hydrocarbons.Research published in the Journal of Polymers and the Environment examined the environmental performance of this type of hydrothermal treatment using data modelled on the Teesside facility. The study estimated a global warming impact of 478kg of CO₂ equivalent per tonne of input plastic and found that the process could have about 80% lower climate impacts than incinerating comparable waste. However, the researchers also identified electricity consumption as a major contributor to the process's environmental impact. This is one reason the technology is different from simply putting plastic through a furnace. The plastic itself is not directly combusted. The aim is to recover its chemical building blocks so they can remain within the manufacturing system.A 20,000-tonne-a-year starting pointAccording to Mura Technology, it started its first commercial plant known as HydroPRS at Wilton in October 2023 and initiated its commissioning process. In the beginning, the capacity of the first plant would generate 20,000 tonnes of recycled liquid hydrocarbon products per annum, although there was enough capacity at the site to triple this figure. The company further stated that the first recycled hydrocarbon products would be ready to be supplied to their commercial partners in 2024. These products are not just simple plastic pellets. Some fractions of the hydrocarbons generated could be used as raw materials for petrochemicals and replace a portion of the naphtha used to manufacture plastics from fossil fuels.Balancing carbon savings with energy costsAn environmental benefit of the technology is linked to what happens to plastic that would otherwise be burned rather than chemically recycled. Reuters reported in 2023 that the company estimated that treating each tonne of plastic could avoid about 1.8 tonnes of CO₂ emissions by preventing the waste from being burned. The life-cycle analysis produced a broadly similar result. It found a global warming impact of 478 kg of CO₂ equivalent per tonne for hydrothermal treatment, compared with 2,340 kg of CO₂ equivalent for burning a tonne of mixed waste plastic. This represents a difference of about 1.86 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent per tonne of plastic, or roughly an 80% reduction in global warming impact compared with burning.The experiment also highlighted an environmental cost associated with the technology. During the hydrothermal treatment stage, electricity accounted for almost 59% of the process's carbon footprint. The researchers suggested that improving energy efficiency and using lower-carbon electricity could reduce this impact. The Teesside project therefore addresses a specific recycling problem rather than offering a blanket solution for plastic waste. Plastics that are simple to separate can still be mechanically recycled, while more complex materials could potentially be broken down into chemical feedstock. In this sense, the project is not simply about finding another way to dispose of plastic, but about finding a route for difficult waste materials to remain in the production cycle.You use AI every day. articles.title: James Cagney’s former Beverly Hills estate was restored over many years, preserving its original fireplaces and leaded glass; the five-acre compound listed for $38.5 million is now asking $29.995 million
articles.summary: A piece of Hollywood history is back on the Beverly Hills market, but with a considerably smaller price tag.
articles.body: A piece of Hollywood history is back on the Beverly Hills market, but with a considerably smaller price tag. James Cagney’s former estate at 9631 Cedarbrook Drive, a roughly five-acre compound tucked beneath Franklin Canyon, was once listed for $38.5 million and is now asking $29.995 million, according to The Beverly Hills Estates. The property has also undergone years of restoration, with its original fireplaces, leaded glass and other period details carefully retained alongside modern updates. The Christie’s listing highlights how its historic character has been preserved across the sprawling compound, which once served as a private retreat for the celebrated actor.A secluded retreat from HollywoodCagney established the five-acre estate in Beverly Hills in the 1930s. The actor, who lived from 1899 to 1986, became famous for a string of memorable film roles, particularly the tough-guy characters that helped define his screen image. Away from the cameras, however, the estate offered a considerably quieter setting. Set beneath Franklin Canyon, the property has the feel of a private country retreat rather than a conventional celebrity compound. Its large grounds and natural surroundings gave Cagney a degree of separation from the city while still keeping him close to Beverly Hills.The estate has since grown into a substantial residential compound. The current listing puts the living area at about 10,778 square feet, with seven bedrooms, seven full bathrooms and three half-bathrooms.Historic details were kept during the restorationMuch of the interest in the property comes from what has survived from its earlier years. The main villa retains exposed trussed-beam ceilings, leaded glass windows, reclaimed European terracotta roof tiles and original fireplaces that have been restored. Rather than replacing those features with an entirely contemporary interior, the restoration appears to have been approached with the property's history in mind. Christie’s describes years of work on the estate, with updated finishes incorporated alongside older architectural elements.Inside, the house includes a wine cellar, kitchen, formal dining room and living areas that open towards shaded terraces. Reclaimed 19th-century French oak is also among the materials used in the restoration, bringing another historic element into the interiors. The compound is not limited to the main residence. It includes a guest residence, a carriage house and a separate guest cottage. That cottage has an especially personal connection to Cagney because it was originally used as his art studio. Cagney’s interest in painting is another side of the actor that is often less prominent than his film career, making the preserved studio an unusual part of the property’s story.More than just a large Beverly Hills houseThe layout of the estate is one of its defining features. Several buildings are connected by stone pathways, gardens and courtyards, creating a collection of spaces rather than making the property feel like one oversized mansion. There is also plenty built into the grounds for recreation and entertaining. The estate has a regulation tennis court, pickleball court and half basketball court, along with a swimming pool and spa. Outdoor chef’s kitchens and a poolside cabana add to the entertaining spaces.Yet it is the surrounding landscape that gives the compound much of its character. The estate is set in a canyon setting surrounded by natural landscape. At the same time, the estate remains close to the centre of Beverly Hills. Landscaping adds another layer of privacy, with mature greenery surrounding the buildings and a large banyan tree positioned near the motor court.A sizeable price cutThe property's price history changed notably in 2026. It was listed for $38.5 million on February 6 before being withdrawn on June 11. A new listing went live on June 12 with an asking price of $29.995 million. The reduction puts the estate back on the market at a price nearly $8.5 million below its earlier asking figure.But the property is being presented as more than a luxury home with a long list of amenities. Its connection to Cagney, the age of the main residence and the restoration of its period features give it a story that a newly constructed mansion cannot easily replicate. Nearly a century after Cagney made the estate his home, the compound still combines the privacy of a large hillside property with access to Beverly Hills. Its restored fireplaces, leaded glass, old timber and former art studio offer reminders of the people and period that shaped the estate, while the newer amenities make the sprawling property suited to contemporary use.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: In 2021, a California couple bought a home and faced more than $1 million in fines linked to the previous owner's cannabis operation; five years later, a settlement cleared the disputed penalties
articles.summary: When Corrine and Doug Thomas bought a property in Humboldt County, California, in 2021, they expected to take ownership of a home and land.
articles.body: When Corrine and Doug Thomas bought a property in Humboldt County, California, in 2021, they expected to take ownership of a home and land. Instead, they inherited a legal dispute connected to the previous owner’s alleged cannabis operation. County officials sought more than $1 million in penalties against the couple, along with roughly $200,000 to demolish a barn where cannabis had reportedly been grown. Five years later, a settlement has withdrawn the disputed notices, fines and fees. The Institute for Justice said the agreement also requires Humboldt County to reform its code enforcement process. Court records available through Justia show that the case challenged how the county imposed cannabis-related penalties on property owners who disputed the alleged violations.A home purchase followed by a huge billThe Thomases’ ordeal began after they purchased the property in 2021. According to the Institute for Justice, Humboldt County treated conditions linked to the previous owner’s cannabis activity as violations that continued to affect the property after the sale. The couple said they had not committed the alleged violations and were not responsible for the earlier operation. Yet the county pursued penalties against them based on the property’s history and the structures located on the land.The financial exposure grew quickly. The Thomases faced more than $1 million in civil penalties, as well as an estimated $200,000 cost to demolish a barn behind the home. For a newly arrived property owner, the potential liability was far greater than an ordinary code violation fine.The case raised a basic question about property ownership. Should a buyer be held financially responsible for alleged activity conducted by someone else before the buyer acquired the land?How the county’s fine system workedHumboldt County’s cannabis code enforcement system allowed penalties to accumulate on a daily basis. According to reports about the lawsuit, fines could reach $10,000 or $12,000 per day, depending on the violation and the applicable county rules.The Institute for Justice argued that the system effectively placed the burden on property owners to prove their innocence. Attorneys said county officials used satellite images and other indicators to identify suspected unpermitted cannabis activity, sometimes without fully investigating who had carried out the work or when it had occurred. Once a violation notice was issued, the penalties could continue while the owner waited for a hearing. That created a serious financial problem for people who wanted to challenge the allegations, because the amount at stake could grow dramatically before they had an opportunity to present evidence.For the Thomases, the county’s position meant that buying the property had not ended the previous owner’s alleged legal problems. Instead, the consequences followed the land and became the new owners’ responsibility to contest.A wider group of affected ownersThe Thomases were not the only property owners involved in the lawsuit. The Institute for Justice represented five people who challenged Humboldt County’s enforcement practices. Another plaintiff, Rhonda Olson, reportedly faced proposed penalties totalling millions of dollars on properties she purchased after earlier cannabis activity had ended.The case also involved property owners who said they were accused of violations they did not commit, as per reports. One plaintiff, Blu Graham, waited years for a hearing to show that a greenhouse on his property was being used for vegetables rather than cannabis, according to reporting about the case. The different circumstances shared a common concern. The owners said county officials treated satellite images, property features or past activity as sufficient evidence of violations, while failing to provide a prompt process for correcting mistakes.The lawsuit argued that excessive fines and delayed hearings violated constitutional protections, including the Eighth Amendment’s prohibition on excessive fines and due process guarantees.The legal battle lasted four yearsThe property owners filed the federal lawsuit in 2022. The litigation continued as the plaintiffs challenged the county’s enforcement framework and the way penalties were imposed. The case did not immediately end when the property owners asked courts to intervene. The U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear a petition concerning whether the plaintiffs were entitled to a jury trial in the proceedings.However, the lawsuit continued in the federal courts. The Ninth Circuit allowed claims concerning excessive fines to move forward after finding that the property owners had plausibly alleged that the county’s practices violated constitutional protections.That ruling increased pressure on the county to resolve the dispute. Rather than continue through a full trial, Humboldt County entered into a settlement with the plaintiffs.What the settlement changesUnder the agreement, Humboldt County will withdraw all outstanding cannabis-related notices of violation, fines and fees challenged by the five property owners. That means the Thomases will no longer face the more than $1 million in penalties linked to the property. The county also agreed to pay $350,000 towards the plaintiffs’ expenses and attorneys’ fees. The payment is not described as an admission of wrongdoing by the county. The settlement requires several changes to the enforcement process. Before imposing future cannabis-related penalties, the county must provide property owners with a warning and 30 days to respond. Owners will also be entitled to a hearing within 60 days. Fines will not continue accumulating while the hearing process is pending, addressing one of the central concerns raised by the plaintiffs. The federal court will retain jurisdiction over the settlement for three years. That gives the court authority to address disputes over whether the county follows the agreed reforms.Why the case matters to homeownersThe case shows how property-related penalties can create serious risks for buyers. A homeowner may purchase land without knowing that a prior owner’s activities could later trigger fines, demolition demands or legal action.It also highlights the importance of due process in local code enforcement. Governments have authority to regulate buildings, land use and cannabis cultivation, but property owners need a meaningful opportunity to understand allegations and challenge them before penalties become overwhelming. The settlement does not prevent Humboldt County from enforcing its cannabis rules. Instead, it changes when and how the county can impose penalties, requiring advance notice and a timely hearing.For the Thomases, the agreement brings an end to a financial threat connected to a property they did not own when the alleged cannabis activity occurred. For other homeowners, the reforms may prevent a similar situation from lasting for years.A new chapter for the property ownersThe settlement clears the disputed penalties and removes the immediate threat of a million-dollar bill from the Thomases’ home. It also ends a legal struggle that began soon after they purchased the property and continued for roughly four years. The broader lesson is that code enforcement can affect more than the person accused of violating a rule. When fines attach to land, later buyers can become involved even if they had no role in the conduct that prompted the penalties.Humboldt County’s revised process now requires the government to communicate with owners before issuing fines and to provide a prompt forum for disputes. Whether those reforms work as intended will be monitored over the next three years.For Corrine and Doug Thomas, however, the immediate outcome is clear. The penalties tied to the former owner’s alleged cannabis operation have been withdrawn, allowing the couple to keep their home without carrying a financial burden created before they ever bought it.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Message of hope': California becomes 18th US state to ban child marriage
articles.summary: California has officially banned child marriage after Governor Gavin Newsom signed legislation setting 18 as the minimum age for marriage and domestic
articles.body: California has officially banned child marriage after Governor Gavin Newsom signed legislation setting 18 as the minimum age for marriage and domestic partnerships in the state.Assembly Bill 1267, authored by Democratic Assemblywoman Gail Pellerin of Santa Cruz, repeals provisions that previously allowed minors to marry with parental consent and court approval. The law will come into effect on January 1, 2027.California ends exceptions for minorsNewsom signed the legislation on Wednesday alongside media personality and child marriage survivor Courtney Stodden, who was allowed by her parents to marry actor Doug Hutchison when she was 16 and he was 51.“This is a long overdue measure to protect young Californians and minors. Today, California kids are safer than ever before,” Newsom said, according to NBC Los Angeles.The legislation was sponsored by Unchained at Last and the California Commission on the Status of Women and Girls. California had previously been among the US states without a statutory minimum marriage age.Under the earlier law, minors could marry if they had parental consent and court approval. The law also provided no mechanism for people under 18 to obtain a divorce.Survivors welcome new lawStodden, who has campaigned against child marriage, described the legislation as a “victory” and said she would continue campaigning until children were protected from marriage across all 50 states.“Governor Newsom's action today made clear to me and to survivors of child marriage everywhere that we should never have been expected to carry this burden,” Stodden said, according to NBC Los Angeles.She also spoke about feelings of guilt associated with her experience.“Today really taught me something. It taught me that what happened to me and to these other girls was wrong. And I was never the problem,” Stodden told NBC Los Angeles.Other survivors also welcomed the legislation. Brittany Bee, who told the BBC she was married at 17 after trying to escape an abusive home, said, “California has sent a clear message to the world today. A message of hope for all children that they may be free from systemic violence. That they may choose their own path.”How common was child marriage in California?Global Hope 365 said around 35,000 marriages involving minors took place in California between 2000 and 2021, with most involving an underage girl and an adult man, according to NBC Los Angeles.Advocacy group Unchained At Last estimated that about 9,000 girls were married each year in California and said almost all child marriages involved girls marrying adult men.Rima Nashashibi, founder and president of Global Hope 365 and founder of the California Coalition to End Child Marriage, said survivors had been central to the campaign for a ban.“The heart of this effort has always been the survivors,” Pellerin said. “They told us what it means to be a child in a marriage you did not freely choose.”California becomes 18th US state to ban child marriageCalifornia is the 18th US state to completely ban child marriage since 2018. The practice remains legal in 32 states, although some have set minimum ages below 18 under specific conditions.Mississippi and New Mexico do not have a statutory minimum age, while other states permit marriage below 18 in certain circumstances.Stodden said she now wanted to focus on Nevada, where she was married at 16. “After I got married in Nevada, they upped it to 17, but that's not good enough for me,” she said.The new California law will take effect on January 1, 2027, after which people must be at least 18 to marry in the state.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2022, a Connecticut couple bought a cottage on 50 acres and built forest trails; after charging visitors to walk there, they faced a zoning dispute and are fighting to reopen their land to hikers
articles.summary: A Connecticut couple who bought 50 acres of land in Roxbury in 2022 is fighting a zoning dispute after town officials told them they could not continue
articles.body: A Connecticut couple who bought 50 acres of land in Roxbury in 2022 is fighting a zoning dispute after town officials told them they could not continue allowing hikers and dog owners to use their private forest trails for a fee.According to CT Mirror, Charles and Eli Copley had bought the property with plans to renovate an old cottage and manage the surrounding woodland. The couple worked with a forester to develop a forest management plan. The work included removing rubbish, deteriorating hunting structures and invasive species from the property. They also built a trail system through the woods to improve access for managing the land and eventually created about 1.3 miles of trails.The Copleys also wanted regular foot traffic to help control low-growing vegetation on the trails. Therefore, in 2024, they listed the property on Sniffspot, an online platform that allows people to rent private properties by the hour for dog walking. The Copleys charged $10 an hour and also allowed hikers to use the trails.The arrangement was meant to help maintain the trails and recover some of the costs of managing the forest. The property received about two or three bookings a week while the listing was active.Officials raise zoning concernsThe arrangement continued for several months before the Copleys received a letter from the Roxbury Land Use Department in April 2025. The letter warned of a possible zoning violation and referred to the property as a “dog park”. It also included requirements for operating a “home enterprise” and advised the couple to stop renting out the property until the requirements were met.The Copleys initially tried to work with the town. They applied for permission to rent out the trails and spent months discussing the issue with officials. According to the couple, they were eventually told that they would need to combine the two parcels making up their property into one lot.The couple said doing so would require expensive surveys and could affect their ability to build a second house on the property. They did not agree to consolidate the parcels. They also explored changes to the town's zoning rules but remained unable to find a way to reopen the trails.Copleys challenge town's interpretationThe Institute for Justice, which is representing the Copleys, said the couple stopped taking reservations after receiving the town's notice and spent more than a year trying to resolve the issue.In August, attorneys for the Copleys sent a letter to Roxbury officials demanding that the couple be allowed to rent parts of the property for recreation or be given an explanation of why the activity violates local zoning rules.“The town has been unable to explain how allowing people to walk outside on private property could possibly be problematic, and that’s because there is no reason,” said John Korevec, an attorney with the Institute for Justice.“The Copleys have done this before without incident, and to our knowledge, there’s been no complaints,” Korevec added. “Zoning codes are supposed to prevent genuine nuisances, not punish peaceful people who are doing nothing wrong. That’s zoning abuse,” he said.Charles questiones why allowing people to walk on the forest had become such a difficult issue. “I just kept thinking, like, how can this be so hard with something as innocuous as this? Like, if I can’t do this, can anybody do anything?” he asked during a virtual press conference on August 27.The Institute for Justice argues that the couple's forest management plan included low-impact recreation and that the town's zoning rules allow agricultural and forestry uses as well as certain accessory uses. It also points to similar uses on land managed by a local land trust.The organisation further argues that the couple's activity is different from a conventional home-based business because people are using outdoor trails rather than operating inside the house.Appeal keeps dispute openTim Hollister, a land use attorney at the Hartford firm Hinckley Allen, told CT Mirror that home enterprise rules are common in Connecticut zoning codes and are often used for businesses such as a small medical office operating from a home.However, he said he had not heard of such rules being applied to outdoor activities. “It doesn’t occur inside your house, so it’s not a home enterprise,” Hollister said.He also noted that other issues, including parking or portable restroom access, could potentially raise separate zoning questions. “It may be something else, but it’s not the general understanding of the term home enterprise,” he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Meet Hudson Lightfoot, the 16-year-old Orillia teen who started window cleaning with a bucket and squeegee at 13, then grew it to 125 clients, hired employees and won a $3,000 business grant
articles.summary: At 16, Hudson Lightfoot is balancing high school with a business he started when he was just 13.
articles.body: At 16, Hudson Lightfoot is balancing high school with a business he started when he was just 13. What began as a simple window-cleaning operation in Orillia has since grown into Marchmont Window Cleaning, a student-owned business serving customers across the area. According to OrilliaMatters, Lightfoot has built a client base of 125 customers, hired his first employees and received a $3,000 grant through Ontario’s Summer Company programme. Marchmont Window Cleaning's website describes the company as a student-owned, locally operated business established in 2023.From a bucket and squeegee to a growing businessLightfoot told OrilliaMatters that he started the business at 13 with a bucket and squeegee. At the time, the operation was a small venture run by a teenager looking to earn money while learning how to manage a business. He reinvested his first summer's earnings into the company. OrilliaMatters reports that Lightfoot used the money to purchase a water-purification hose system, allowing him to clean windows as high as four storeys without relying on traditional ladder work.The system also became part of the business's environmental approach. Lightfoot told OrilliaMatters that the system uses water rather than harsh chemicals or soaps. Marchmont Window Cleaning's website similarly describes its water-fed pole system as using purified water without chemical cleaning agents. The company's website now lists several services beyond window cleaning, including interior and exterior window cleaning, gutter cleaning, gutter brightening, siding soft washing and hard-water stain removal. It says the business serves Orillia and communities across Simcoe County and Muskoka.125 clients and the first employeesThe business did not remain a one-person operation. OrilliaMatters reports that Lightfoot's client base has grown from zero to 125, with many customers returning for additional services. That repeat business has been an important part of the company's growth. In his own LinkedIn posts, Lightfoot has described learning about sales, customer service, pricing and operations through the business. He has also written about the transition from working alone to becoming responsible for other people's work. “I hired my first employees this summer,” Lightfoot told OrilliaMatters. He added that the community had been supportive of the business. His LinkedIn profile also describes the same change, saying that the business moved from being “just me and a squeegee” to having employees. He wrote that hiring made training and systems more important as the company expanded.A $3,000 grant helped him expandAnother step came through Ontario's Summer Company programme. OrilliaMatters reports that Lightfoot received a $3,000 grant this summer through the Summer Company Program administered locally through the Small Business Centre of Barrie, Simcoe County and Orillia. The provincial programme provides eligible student entrepreneurs with financial support and business guidance. Ontario's official programme information says successful applicants can receive up to $3,000, with the money divided between start-up support and completion of programme requirements. Lightfoot told OrilliaMatters that he used the grant to register and insure the business, buy marketing materials and purchase additional equipment. Those investments allowed him to expand the operation and bring in his first employees. His LinkedIn profile also identifies him as a 2026 Summer Company Grant Recipient and lists the Government of Ontario among his honours and awards.Learning business while still in schoolRunning a company has also meant learning skills that do not necessarily come from a classroom. On LinkedIn, Lightfoot describes Marchmont Window Cleaning as a place where he is learning about sales, operations, hiring, pricing and customer service. He has also taught himself coding. He initially created a free website for the business before learning coding to build a more advanced website and create an app for the company.Marchmont Window Cleaning's website reflects that development. It presents the business as a student-owned service company, offers online quote requests and promotes several cleaning services throughout the region. For Lightfoot, however, the business is not his only pursuit. OrilliaMatters reports that he is also a competitive freestyle skier and certified coach during the winter. His LinkedIn profile likewise lists competitive skiing among his activities.A teenage business built one customer at a timeLightfoot's story began with basic equipment and a teenager willing to knock on doors to find customers. Three years later, Marchmont Window Cleaning has grown to 125 clients, added employees and expanded its range of services. What started with a bucket and squeegee has therefore become more than a summer job. It has given Lightfoot experience with customers, equipment, marketing, technology and managing a team, all while he continues his education.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Pete Hegseth to cut generals & admirals in US military by 20%; Pentagon to create new drone command
articles.summary: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has announced plans to cut the number of generals and admirals in the US military by 20 per cent, while unveiling a new
articles.body: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has announced plans to cut the number of generals and admirals in the US military by 20 per cent, while unveiling a new four-star command focused on autonomous and robotic warfare.According to news agency AP, Hegseth made the announcements during his “State of the Force” address at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia on Wednesday. He said the military services would double a 10% reduction ordered last spring for roughly 800 flag and general officer positions, bringing the total planned reduction to 20% by January 1, 2027.“I call it accountability and long overdue,” Hegseth said while announcing the cuts.The Pentagon chief also announced plans to create a new four-star command to oversee the development and deployment of autonomous and robotic military capabilities. He described the move as part of what he called the “fastest peacetime shift in modern military history.”Hegseth said the US military needed to adapt to the changing nature of warfare, pointing to the growing use of drones on battlefields, including in Ukraine and the ongoing conflict with Iran.“Ukraine’s lesson is not that one type of drone wins wars, but rather the need for a purpose-built system that maximizes the ability to adapt,” Hegseth said.The announcement comes after a US Army unit in Europe that specialised in drone warfare was recently ordered to end its efforts and return to its traditional role as an infantry battalion. A bipartisan group of lawmakers subsequently asked the Army to explain the decision, citing the increasing importance of uncrewed systems in modern warfare.Hegseth faces criticism over military leadership cutsThe planned reduction in senior military positions has drawn questions from members of Congress. Some lawmakers have described the move as a purge of the military's top ranks and warned that rebuilding the leadership structure could take years.Democratic Senator Mark Kelly, a former Navy combat pilot and NASA astronaut, criticised Hegseth's approach to military leadership.“He’s purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it’s going to take a generation to recover from it,” Kelly said.Republican Senator Mike Rounds, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he wanted to understand the reasoning behind the cuts.“If it’s simply a matter of eliminating a very heavy top, there may be some validity to it, but I want to see it first,” Rounds said.Musk, Gingrich to study future of warfareHegseth also announced a study on the future of warfare involving SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, former Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Palmer Luckey, co-founder of defence technology company Anduril Industries.He said the initiative would focus on developing weapons and systems needed for future battlefields, including technologies capable of operating across a range of environments.The Pentagon chief also announced plans for a new military base, inviting all 50 US states to compete to host between 15,000 and 25,000 service members. Another proposal would make every US military base self-powered.The announcements form part of Hegseth’s broader effort to restructure the US military and shift its focus towards what he describes as war-fighting capabilities.You use AI every day. articles.title: Indian-origin truck driver jailed for 6 years in Canada after fatal crash that killed mom, 11-year-old son
articles.summary: A Quebec court sentenced Baljeet Singh to six years in prison after admitting to playing a mobile game that led to a tragic crash, killing a mother and her son. Singh, 30, caused a seven-vehicle pileup while distracted by his phone, resulting in multiple injuries and fatalities.
articles.body: An Indian-origin truck driver has been sentenced to six years in prison in Canada after admitting that he was playing a mobile game when his tractor-trailer caused a crash that killed a mother and her 11-year-old son.Quebec Court Judge Sacha Blais sentenced Baljeet Singh, who turns 30 on Saturday, at Longueuil courthouse on Wednesday, according to French-language media outlet Noovo Info.With credit for time already spent in custody, Singh will serve four years, four months and four days. He has also been banned from driving for 10 years.Singh pleaded guilty in April to dangerous driving causing death and dangerous driving causing bodily harm. The charges stemmed from a seven-vehicle pileup on Highway 30 in Brossard on July 19, 2022.Nancy Lefrançois, 42, died at the scene, while her son, Loïc Chevalier, 11, died in hospital. Several other people were injured.Singh was driving a 53-foot tractor-trailer as traffic slowed near a construction zone close to Grande-Allée Boulevard. He admitted that he was playing Ludo on his phone and was not watching the road when the collision occurred.The judge described Singh's use of the phone as an aggravating factor and said his conduct showed disregard for other people's lives.“Using [the phone] to play a video game shows a total lack of judgment,” Blais said.Singh's guilty plea, lack of previous convictions and expressions of remorse were considered mitigating factors. The judge said his remorse appeared sincere but placed the sentence towards the upper end of the applicable range because of the consequences of the crash.The court also heard that Singh initially met investigators voluntarily after the collision and said he could not remember what had happened. He then left for India and deleted his social media accounts, according to an agreed statement of facts presented in court.A Canada-wide arrest warrant was issued in 2024. Singh was arrested in the United States on August 21 last year before being returned to Canada.After his return, Singh acknowledged to Quebec police that he had been playing Ludo when the crash happened and accepted responsibility.Evidence from his truck's dashboard camera also showed more than 40 traffic violations during his final three trips. Investigators said he repeatedly used his cellphone while driving, changed lanes improperly and exceeded permitted driving hours by failing to take mandatory rest periods.Lefrancois's husband, Benoit Lavoie, was also seriously injured. He suffered a collapsed lung, fractured ribs, a concussion, head trauma and scalp injuries, and spent three weeks in a coma.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Two California men allegedly created medical-equipment companies with no storefronts or warehouses, billed Medicare for $3.5 million and switched to a new company whenever fraud checks began denying the old one’s claims
articles.summary: Two California men allegedly created a series of medical-equipment companies with no physical storefronts or warehouses, used them to submit more than
articles.body: Two California men allegedly created a series of medical-equipment companies with no physical storefronts or warehouses, used them to submit more than $3.5 million in fraudulent claims to Medicare and moved on to new companies when the previous ones began facing fraud-related claim denials, according to the U.S. Department of Justice. The case involves Nouman Mustafa, 36, of Torrance, and Mohsin Khan, 40, of Bakersfield, who were indicted by a federal grand jury on September 17 on multiple counts of health care fraud and aggravated identity theft. The charges were announced by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of California.Companies allegedly created to appear legitimateAccording to court records cited by the Justice Department, Mustafa and Khan allegedly created a series of shell companies between January 2025 and January 2026. The businesses were designed to appear to be legitimate durable medical equipment (DME) companies that could provide medical equipment to Medicare beneficiaries. Investigators allege that the companies did not actually operate like genuine medical-equipment businesses. None of them had physical storefronts, warehouses or other locations where legitimate business could have been conducted, according to the court records.The two men allegedly used the companies to submit claims to Medicare for durable medical equipment. In total, the claims they submitted amounted to more than $3.5 million, prosecutors said. The alleged operation was also structured to move from one company to another. Mustafa and Khan typically used a company for only a few weeks or months. Once its claims began to be denied because of suspected fraud, they allegedly shifted their activity to another company and continued submitting claims.Information allegedly came from contacts overseasThe Justice Department alleges that Mustafa and Khan obtained information used to submit the claims from contacts in Pakistan and elsewhere. The information reportedly included details belonging to real Medicare beneficiaries as well as information about their doctors. The men allegedly used those details as part of the process of submitting the fraudulent claims to the federal health insurance programme.According to prosecutors, Mustafa and Khan did not keep all the proceeds generated through the alleged scheme. They allegedly retained approximately 30% of the money, while sending the remaining amount to their contacts. The allegations describe a scheme that prosecutors say relied on a succession of companies rather than a single business entity. When one company's claims attracted scrutiny and began to be rejected, the defendants allegedly moved to another company, allowing the alleged billing activity to continue.Arrests and federal investigationThe case came under investigation by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General, with assistance from the Bakersfield Police Department, according to the Justice Department. Mustafa was arrested on February 11, 2026, at Los Angeles International Airport while he was attempting to board a one-way flight to Pakistan. At that time, he was arrested on a criminal complaint.Khan was arrested at his home in Bakersfield on September 30, the same day the Justice Department announced the indictment. He was scheduled to make his initial court appearance following his arrest. According to the Justice Department, the two men are Pakistani nationals who also hold dual United States citizenship. Court records indicate that they had previously worked in the US in occupations including security guards, warehouse managers and licensed insurance agents.Charges and potential penaltiesMustafa and Khan face multiple counts of health care fraud and aggravated identity theft. If convicted, each health care fraud count carries a potential sentence of up to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000. The aggravated identity theft charges carry a mandatory minimum sentence of two years in prison, which would be served consecutively to any sentence imposed for the other counts, according to the Justice Department. However, the eventual sentences, if there are convictions, would be determined by the court after consideration of applicable statutory factors and the federal Sentencing Guidelines. The case remains at the charging stage. The Justice Department stressed that the allegations contained in the indictment are not findings of guilt and that Mustafa and Khan are presumed innocent unless and until they are proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.You use AI every day.
