articles.title: Martin Margiela's first portfolio for his future fashion house was stolen on a train; 39 years later, it sold for €24,700
articles.summary: A portfolio Martin Margiela created in 1987 while developing the idea for his future fashion house was stolen on a train and recovered by police a year
articles.body: A portfolio Martin Margiela created in 1987 while developing the idea for his future fashion house was stolen on a train and recovered by police a year later. Nearly four decades later, the portfolio was offered at auction in Paris in July, as part of a sale drawn from Margiela's personal archives. Described by Maurice Auction as the first portfolio illustrating the future Maison Martin Margiela, the 1987 dossier contains 13 A3-format pages of drawings, facsimiles and collages setting out the aesthetic of the then-unnamed house. Estimated at €5,000 to €8,000, it sold for €24,700 at the July 9, 2026 sale, including fees. The archive sale also brought together sketches, prototypes, garments and personal objects spanning Margiela’s career and later years at Hermès.Martin Margiela's 1987 portfolio captured the idea behind his future fashion houseThe portfolio dates to the period before Maison Martin Margiela was established in 1988. In his note accompanying the auction lot, Margiela recalled that he was looking for a manufacturer in Italy and needed to visualise the fashion he wanted to create. He drew silhouettes and accessories for his imagined fashion house and assembled them in a white cotton-covered folder. Maurice Auction describes the resulting dossier as the first portfolio illustrating the future Maison Martin Margiela and says its 13 A3-format pages of drawings, facsimiles and collages set out the house's aesthetic.The folder was later stolen on a train. Margiela made another version for his travels, using photocopies of the drawings. He recalled that he considered the photocopies more contemporary than the original pencil sketches and was able to create an almost identical portfolio. A year later, police recovered the stolen folder, after which Margiela compared the two versions and was struck by their similarity. The auction catalogue gives the provenance of the portfolio offered for sale as Margiela's personal archives, but does not specify whether the lot was the recovered original or the replacement.The archive sale traced Margiela's career from 1984 onwardsThe 1987 portfolio was part of a wider sale of Margiela's personal archives organised by Maurice Auction in collaboration with Kerry Taylor Auctions. The auction house said the material covered the period from 1984 to 2008 and included photographs, drawings and objects, alongside some pieces made during the pandemic. The sale brought together material from different stages of Margiela's career, including work from before the creation of his own fashion house.Among the earliest material were pieces associated with the Golden Spindle competition in Antwerp. Maurice Auction's English catalogue uses “Golden Spindle” as the translation of the French Canette d'Or. The archive included sketches, prototypes and presentation material connected with this early period. The auction also included a fashion drawing from Paris dated 1985. Estimated at €1,500 to €2,000, the drawing sold for €18,200. The archive extended into Margiela's later career and his period at Hermès, where he was responsible for the women's collections from 1997 to 2003. Among the personal objects offered was a white cotton working blouse from Margiela's personal archives, catalogued as dating from 1988–2008. The auction catalogue says the blouse was signed ‘Martin’ by the designer and bears substantial paint marks consistent with its use as workwear. Estimated at €6,000 to €10,000, it sold for €41,600.The graffiti Tabi boots became the sale's top resultAnother major lot was a pair of white-painted Tabi ankle boots associated with the 1991 Palais Galliera exhibition The World According to Its Creators. The exhibition invited visitors to write messages on its white-painted walls and floor. According to Margiela's account in the auction catalogue, visitors also unexpectedly wrote on the white-painted Tabi boots, leaving them covered in graffiti. This makes it more accurate to say that the boots were displayed at the exhibition and subsequently covered with writing by visitors, rather than describing the graffiti as something specifically created for the exhibition.Estimated at €30,000 to €50,000, the Tabi boots achieved a result of €364,000 including fees. Maurice Auction's sale information states that buyer fees were 25% excluding tax, or 30% including tax. On that basis, the corresponding hammer price would be approximately €280,000, although that figure is a calculation rather than the auction house's published result. The sale also included later pieces in which Margiela revisited his earlier work. Lot 46 was a one-of-a-kind sweater made from grey cotton socks, inspired by his Autumn-Winter 1991–1992 collection and created by the designer around 2020. Estimated at €25,000 to €40,000, it sold for €117,000. articles.title: A pair of gold Jordans was donated to an Oregon shelter; later found to be custom-made for Spike Lee, they sold for $50,800
articles.summary: A pair of striking gold Nike Air Jordan 3 sneakers ended up in a donation bin at the Portland Rescue Mission in Oregon in 2023, where staff initially
articles.body: A pair of striking gold Nike Air Jordan 3 sneakers ended up in a donation bin at the Portland Rescue Mission in Oregon in 2023, where staff initially suspected they were counterfeit. The shoes had been anonymously donated and were discovered by James Free, a man participating in the shelter's long-term programme, while he was sorting through donated items. Their unusual appearance eventually prompted staff to seek expert authentication. The sneakers turned out to be part of a tiny batch of custom Air Jordan 3s created by Nike designer Tinker Hatfield for filmmaker Spike Lee and people in his inner circle. After being authenticated, the rare shoes were put up for auction by Sotheby's and sold for $50,800 in December 2023.Rare Spike Lee Jordans discovered in donation binThe sneakers were placed in a donation chute at the Portland Rescue Mission's Burnside Shelter in April 2023. They eventually made their way into a basement donation bin containing clothing, blankets, coats, sleeping bags and shoes.James Free, who was living in the Mission's long-term shelter programme at the time, spotted the bright gold sneakers near the bottom of the bin. Their appearance immediately caught his attention, and he brought them to Erin Holcomb, the organisation's director of staff ministry.The shoes were in remarkably good condition. However, the circumstances surrounding their discovery made the staff suspicious. Holcomb initially believed they were likely high-quality fakes and did not immediately realise that the shelter had received an extremely rare pair of sneakers.Why the shoes were linked to Spike LeeThe sneakers were custom-made in 2019 by Nike footwear designer Tinker Hatfield for Spike Lee and members of his inner circle.Lee wore his own pair of the gold Air Jordan 3s at the 2019 Academy Awards. He wore them while attending the ceremony and later while accepting the Oscar for best adapted screenplay for BlacKkKlansman.The Portland pair was not Lee's personal pair. The donated sneakers were size 12½, while Lee has said that he wears a size 9½. They were part of a very limited run, with the Portland Rescue Mission describing them as one of only four or five pairs made for Lee's inner circle.The shoes also carried distinctive details connected to Lee. One heel featured the Jumpman logo, while the other carried the logo of his production company, 40 Acres and a Mule Filmworks. The gold colour and customised design made them unlike ordinary retail Air Jordan releases.Staff initially thought they were fakeHolcomb kept the sneakers for several weeks before taking them to Index, a sneaker consignment shop in Portland, to determine whether they were genuine.According to Holcomb's account, she approached the shop expecting an expert to confirm her suspicion that the shoes were counterfeit. Instead, the inspection produced a very different answer.Terrance Ricketts, co-owner of the store, determined that the shoes were authentic. He recognised their unusual construction, materials and markings and told Holcomb that Nike had produced only a handful of them. He estimated that they could be worth between $15,000 and $20,000.That discovery changed the Mission's plans for the shoes. Rather than distributing them as ordinary donated footwear, staff began looking for a way to authenticate and sell them while directing the proceeds towards the organisation's work.Tinker Hatfield authenticated the sneakersThe Mission then contacted Sotheby's, the international auction house, which agreed to handle the sale.Hatfield, who had designed the sneakers, also became involved. He authenticated the shoes and provided additional items for the auction, including a replacement box and an original design concept board. He also visited the Portland Rescue Mission and signed the materials connected to the sneakers.Sotheby's listed the sneakers with an estimated value of $15,000 to $20,000. The auction house also waived its seller's fee, allowing the proceeds from the sale to benefit the Portland Rescue Mission.The identity of the person who originally donated the shoes remained unknown. Even Lee said he did not know how the size 12½ pair had ended up in the shelter's donation system.The auction ends at $50,800The auction produced a much higher result than the initial estimate.As the Sotheby's auction approached its conclusion in December 2023, staff at the Portland Rescue Mission gathered to watch the bidding. The amount eventually climbed sharply during the final minutes.The winning bid reached $50,800, more than twice Sotheby's initial high estimate of $20,000. Staff members at the Mission watched the final moments together and celebrated when the auction closed.The Portland Rescue Mission said the money would support its work helping people experiencing homelessness, including providing shelter, meals, clothing and other services.From a donation bin to a $50,800 auctionWhat made the discovery unusual was the chain of events behind it. A pair of highly limited sneakers connected to one of Hollywood's best-known filmmakers had been anonymously donated to a homeless shelter and ended up buried beneath ordinary donated goods.The shoes were initially mistaken for fakes, then identified by a sneaker expert, authenticated by their original designer and ultimately sold at a major international auction house.The original donor was never identified, but the unexpected donation generated $50,800 for the Portland Rescue Mission, turning an overlooked pair of sneakers at the bottom of a donation bin into a substantial source of funding for the shelter.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2001, the Indian Mesa wind farm began operating in Pecos County with 125 turbines; sheep grazing continued, and $930,000 was paid in school taxes
articles.summary: In May 2001, the Indian Mesa wind farm began operating in Pecos County, West Texas, with 125 turbines and a total installed capacity of 82.5 MW.
articles.body: In May 2001, the Indian Mesa wind farm began operating in Pecos County, West Texas, with 125 turbines and a total installed capacity of 82.5 MW. The project sits on a mesa where the uses of the land include grazing livestock, primarily sheep, and hunting, and the project does not limit these uses. According to the US Government Accountability Office (GAO), the project paid about $930,000 in local school district taxes in 2003. The details appear in report GAO-04-756, published in September 2004, which summarises visits to nine wind power projects in five states.When did the Indian Mesa wind farm in Texas begin operatingThe Indian Mesa project is in Pecos County, Texas, and is owned by FPL Energy, a company based in Florida. The report states that the project started operating in May 2001 and has 125 turbines, with a total installed capacity of 82.5 MW. The GAO lists the power purchasers as the Lower Colorado River Authority and Texas Utilities Company, and records four landowners.The GAO states that "the Indian Mesa wind farm is located in West Texas, an area with strong, sustained wind resources." The report gives an annual generation estimate of 250 million kWh for the project. In its wider findings, the GAO notes that California and Texas accounted for about one-half of the nation's 6,374 MW of installed wind generation capacity at the end of 2003, and its state-by-state figure for Texas is 1,293.0 MW.How much land does the Indian Mesa wind farm occupyThe GAO reports that "the project is located on 34,000 acres situated on a mesa" and that "one of the four landowners of this acreage is the University of Texas." According to the report, "about 7,000 of these acres are leased for the project." It continues: "The uses of the land include grazing livestock, primarily sheep and hunting. The project does not limit these uses."On the wider question of land use, the GAO's introductory letter states that "even large wind turbines use only about a quarter-acre of land each, including access roads, so farmers can continue to plant crops and graze livestock up to the base of the turbines." The report also records that "University of Texas officials indicated that legal and technical resources available to the university were critical to negotiating a favourable lease agreement for a wind project on university property." In its general description of how wind projects are developed, the GAO lists a lease or easement agreement with a term "sufficient for financing the project, usually 25 years or more."How did the project support local training through its tax agreementAccording to the GAO, "as an incentive for locating the project in Pecos County, the county provided the project with a full property tax abatement for 5 years." The report adds that "in return, the project owner (at that time) agreed to donate funds in an amount equivalent to about 10 per cent of the abated taxes to a regional technical training centre." The GAO also states that "the owner also agreed to hire and use local companies and labour for the construction of the project, to the extent possible."The report then records that "the project paid about $930,000 in local school district taxes in 2003." A footnote in the report explains that "because one of the four landowners was a county commissioner, property taxes were assessed for this landowner's parcel to avoid the appearance of a conflict of interest." The GAO does not specify which school districts received the payment in its account of Indian Mesa.How did wind power projects affect Pecos County school tax revenuesAccording to the GAO, "in Pecos County, Texas, with a population of about 16,000 the school districts received about $5 million in 2002 from property tax revenues directly associated with wind power projects in that county." The report states that "the Iraan-Sheffield School District, obtained one-third of its property tax revenues from wind power projects that year" and that "these projects also added about 30 to 35 full-time permanent jobs to operate and maintain the projects." It also cites the Fort Stockton Economic Development Corporation, which said "the county experienced a 10 percent increase in gross sales during the construction of several wind power projects."On employment at Indian Mesa itself, the GAO states that "the project owner currently employs 43 people to operate and maintain the four wind projects the company owns in the area, including the Indian Mesa project." The report continues: "In the future, the owner plans to hire 4 additional people after the warranty and maintenance agreement with the turbine manufacturer expires." Separately, the GAO asked the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) to model hypothetical projects. The GAO asked NREL to model hypothetical scenarios. In one, building a 150 MW project owned by an out-of-area company in Pecos County would create "the equivalent of only 36 full-time jobs for 1 year in the county". That project is nearly twice Indian Mesa's 82.5 MW, and the GAO said it did not expect high accuracy from the model.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 237 vehicles fined for illegal parking on NH in Dhanbad
articles.summary: Dhanbad NH task force fined 237 vehicles Rs 21.5 lakh for illegal roadside parking since Sept 26, launching ongoing enforcement after fatal Sept 24 crash.
articles.body: Dhanbad: The National Highway Task Force has intensified its crackdown on vehicles parked illegally along national highways, collecting around Rs 21.5 lakh in fines from 237 vehicles during a special enforcement drive since Sept 26, officials said on Thursday.The campaign was launched to ensure smooth and safe traffic movement and prevent accidents caused by vehicles parked along busy highway stretches.Officials said several heavy and commercial vehicles were found parked haphazardly on the roadside in violation of traffic regulations, posing a serious risk to motorists.The enforcement drive was conducted jointly by the district transport officer, motor vehicle inspector, district road safety team, police officials and the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) route patrolling vehicle team. The vehicles found violating parking rules were penalised under provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act.Dhanbad DC Aditya Ranjan said the administration was taking the issue of road safety seriously and that the enforcement campaign would continue. He said strict action would be taken against motorists violating traffic regulations.Along with issuing challans, the task force conducted a road safety awareness campaign among drivers and the general public. Drivers were instructed not to park vehicles illegally on national highways or along their edges and to use designated parking areas.Officials said roadside parking, particularly by heavy vehicles, can obstruct traffic movement and reduce visibility for approaching motorists, increasing the possibility of serious accidents.The crackdown has gained significance following the Sept 24 accident in which four children, including Trisha Singh, daughter of rural development minister Deepika Pandey Singh, were killed after their car rammed into a truck parked on the roadside. articles.title: PU marks 109 years without Foundation Day celebrations
articles.summary: Patna University enters 110th year as foundation day events are skipped; officials cite VC’s chancellor meeting, with celebrations to be held later.
articles.body: Patna: A university that once shaped the intellectual, academic and political life of Bihar crossed a historic milestone on Thursday—but without the ceremony that normally marks such an occasion.Patna University (PU), the seventh-oldest university in the Indian subcontinent and Bihar’s first, completed 109 years and entered its 110th year on Oct 1. Yet the campus remained without the foundation day lecture, ceremonial function, gold medal distribution for toppers, or other traditional events associated with the occasion.A senior PU official told TOI that Thursday’s programme could not be held because vice-chancellor Ajay Kumar Singh was scheduled to attend a meeting convened by the chancellor at Lok Bhawan. The official said the celebrations would be held later.The low-key observance drew disappointment from alumni, teachers, students and non-teaching staff, who said the foundation day is a key occasion to reconnect the university community with PU’s history and academic traditions.Former dean of social sciences Nawal Kishore Chaudhary criticised what he called an apathetic approach by the authorities. “The foundation day should be celebrated on the scheduled date,” he said.The absence of celebrations was noted more sharply in light of past practice, when foundation day functions routinely included formal lectures by eminent guests and felicitation of undergraduate toppers with gold medals.The university also did not hold a Teachers’ Day programme on Sept 5 this year, which had previously been observed annually.Established by the Patna University Act, which came into force on Oct 1, 1917, the university initially served as an affiliating and examining authority over a vast educational territory covering Bihar, Odisha and Nepal. articles.title: GAIL told to restore roads after pipeline work
articles.summary: Ranchi administration directs GAIL to restore roads damaged by gas pipeline work, fill pits, add barricading, follow safety norms, and coordinate with NHAI/RCD.
articles.body: Ranchi: The district administration has directed GAIL and its contractors to restore roads damaged during the ongoing gas pipeline works and ensure adequate safety measures at construction sites to prevent inconvenience to commuters.Sadar sub-divisional officer Kumar Rajat, in a meeting with GAIL officials and contractors on Thursday, reviewed the progress of pipeline and road works, restoration of damaged stretches, safety arrangements and adherence to project timelines and issued the directions.Taking cognisance of road damage at several locations due to ongoing pipeline work, DC Manjunath Bhajantri directed GAIL and its contractors to take corrective measures on priority and restore affected roads to their original condition after completion of the work.During the review meeting, Rajat directed contractors to immediately fill pits dug during construction or pipeline laying and ensure that the roads are levelled and made fit for traffic once the work is completed. He stressed that commuters should not be forced to face prolonged inconvenience because of unfinished restoration work.The SDO also instructed contractors to put in place proper barricading and other safety arrangements throughout the duration of the work. Work sites must have measures to facilitate the safe movement of vehicles and pedestrians and prevent accidents, officials said.“Construction and pipeline work should not leave roads in a condition that causes prolonged inconvenience to the public,” Rajat said.He added that contractors would be responsible for the quality of restoration and ensuring that affected roads are traffic-worthy after completion.GAIL officials were also asked to coordinate with National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) and Road Construction Department (RCD) to ensure timely execution of projects and better coordination among agencies.Rajat directed officials and contractors to complete the projects within the stipulated timeframe and regularly monitor the progress of work. articles.title: A North Carolina family bought 600 acres in 1811 and kept part of the land for seven generations; 214 years later, a conservation deal protected 298 acres from becoming housing or commercial developments
articles.summary: A North Carolina family has conserved 298 acres of their land, preserving its historical and environmental significance for future generations. This conservation easement ensures the land remains undeveloped after seven generations of stewardship by the Caldwell-Dietzel family.
articles.body: A North Carolina family has held on to part of the same property for seven generations, more than 200 years after its ancestors bought the land. Now, 298 acres of that historic holding have been placed under permanent conservation protection.The land in Robeson County was purchased by John W. Caldwell and his wife, Nancy Hartfield, in 1811. They had moved from Kinston, North Carolina, to the Raft Swamp area near Lumberton before acquiring the 600-acre property.Last year, on June 9, Three Rivers Land Trust, a non-profit conservation organisation, protected 298 acres of land through a conservation easement, ensuring the property cannot be developed into housing or used for commercial purposes, according to the trust.The agreement covers most of the land that remains with the family today. Of the original 600 acres, 306 acres are still family-owned, with Joe and Rosalie Dietzel and their son, Charles Dietzel, now responsible for its stewardship.The conservation deal means the protected acreage will remain undeveloped rather than being converted into a residential neighbourhood, covered with houses and asphalt or turned into a commercial site.Land passed down through seven generationsThe property has remained connected to the Caldwell-Dietzel family for 214 years, although the way the land has been used has changed over time.More than 200 acres of the property were once cultivated for tobacco. The land is now covered by longleaf and loblolly pine trees and is managed as working forestland.For the family, preserving the property is not only about maintaining the forest. Keeping the land within the family has been one of its key goals.Joe Dietzel said the family wanted to continue the agricultural legacy established by John Caldwell and Nancy Hartfield and eventually pass it to future descendants.“We are deeply honoured and humbled to be able to continue the agricultural legacy of John and Nancy and to pass that legacy on to our descendants,” Dietzel said.The conservation easement gives that intention a permanent legal framework for the 298 acres.While the family retains ownership, the agreement restricts future development of the protected land. It will continue to be used as forestland rather than being opened up for residential or commercial construction.From tobacco farming to pine treesThe landscape has changed significantly since the property was first acquired.Tobacco was once a major part of the family’s use of the land, with more than 200 acres devoted to the crop. Today, longleaf and loblolly pines dominate the property.The family’s management of the forest has also brought recognition from organisations involved in forestry and conservation.The North Carolina Forest Service has recognised the landowners for their efforts to care for the property.The family also became the first landowners from Robeson County to be included in the Longleaf Alliance’s “Longleaf Honour Roll”.That recognition came as the family continued managing the forest while retaining its connection to the property across generations.“The Dietzel family are remarkable stewards of their land and are deeply committed to its permanent conservation,” Emily Callicutt, director of conservation at Three Rivers Land Trust, said.298 acres protected from future developmentThe agreement does not transfer the land to the land trust. Instead, the conservation easement places permanent restrictions on how the 298 acres can be developed.That distinction allows the family to continue owning the property while preventing future development that could fundamentally change its use.The protected acreage will not become a housing development or commercial property. The land will remain undeveloped and continue to showcase the family’s longstanding connection to agriculture and forestry.The agreement also reflects a wider effort by Three Rivers Land Trust to protect family-owned agricultural land.“Saving family farms is one of our core missions,” Travis Morehead, executive director of Three Rivers Land Trust, said. “We understand the significance of agriculture in North Carolina and are proud to help this family conserve their land.”A 214-year connection continuesThe conservation agreement comes more than two centuries after the original 600-acre purchase.Only part of that original holding remains with the family today, but the 306 acres that survived seven generations are still under family stewardship.Of that remaining property, 298 acres are now protected from future development.For the Caldwell-Dietzel family, the deal puts a permanent safeguard around a piece of land that has outlasted generations of owners, changes in agriculture and the transition from tobacco cultivation to managed pine forest.You use AI every day.
